# Verification, Feedback, and Learning {#sec-feedback-verification-trust}

![](images/ch07-cover-map.svg){fig-alt="A returned signal passes through verification qualification and a bounded claim before feedback routes the next action and learning is retained."}

::: {.epigraph}
> "Program testing can be used to show the presence of bugs, but never to show their absence!"
>
> — Edsger W. Dijkstra, *Notes on Structured Programming*, second edition (1970) [@Dijkstra1970Notes, p. 7]
:::

A tool return becomes architectural evidence only after its meaning and limits are established. This chapter connects three jobs. Verification determines which claims a returned measurement or proof can support. Feedback interprets the qualified result and identifies the next action. Learning determines what to improve or retain within the run, across the project, and for later work.

The argument builds on machine-usable representations (@sec-data-representations-world-models), method choice (@sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization), and execution records (@sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces). It distinguishes empirical comparisons from formal proofs, examines proxy error and shared verification blind spots, and connects each result to a justified revision, further check, or stop. Qualified feedback completes the technical foundation of Part II. It supports bounded architectural conclusions and subsequent design work; it does not turn a successful tool run into proof of a complete system.

## Qualified Architectural Actions and Decisions {#sec-from-feedback-to-decision}

When a simulation returns cleanly or a static timing tool reports zero violations, it is tempting to treat the run as an architectural pass. Yet that return may leave an unhandled multicycle path, an unconstrained power domain, or a floating CMOS node[^fn-floating-cmos-c07] unexamined. Generating register-transfer level (RTL) candidates and establishing that they meet their requirements are different jobs. An AI-native design system must determine what its tool returns reveal about those candidates and how the results should guide redesign.

The execution environment described in @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces supplies immutable records with pinned dependencies and raw transcripts. Qualification establishes which claims those returns can support. The required check follows from the claim: physical feasibility requires the relevant physical checks, while a claim of invariant satisfaction requires a proof over its declared model and assumptions. Empirical checks qualify observed quantities from cycle-accurate simulations, hardware emulators, or post-silicon telemetry; formal methods can establish invariant satisfaction over mathematical models under declared assumptions [@Clarke2018ModelChecking]. A particular formal return must still be interpreted: a completed invocation need not mean that the intended obligation was proved.

Translating raw execution logs into architectural choices is a sequence of qualification steps, each of which can send the work back rather than forward (@fig-evidence-flow).

![**Tool returns gain architectural meaning through claim-specific result qualification.** Execution records supply returns with status and lineage; result qualification binds types, targets, and conditions; property checks test formal or physical validity; and feedback scoping defines supported claims before learning records what to revise or retain.](images/fig-evidence-flow){#fig-evidence-flow width="80%" fig-alt="A five-step flow from tool return through verification and a comparison or property check to feedback and a learning step that records what to improve or retain. Side paths send incomplete returns to execution repair and invalid checks to study formulation."}

Qualifying an execution return requires separating five distinct questions:

1. Did the requested tool run execute to completion without infrastructure faults or license drops?
2. Is the returned artifact structurally and syntactically valid for downstream toolchains?
3. Is the measurement or proof valid under its declared model and assumptions, including relevant process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) conditions?
4. Which specific architectural requirement or physical constraint does the result satisfy or contradict, and which requirements remain unexamined?
5. What concrete design revision, parameter update, further check, or bounded claim does the qualified evidence support? Does it instead justify retaining the candidate or stopping work on it?

These distinctions determine what should change next. For example, a license drop calls for execution repair and another run; it supplies no evidence against the candidate. A timing result that omits a required corner calls for completing the check before using it to support timing feasibility. A qualified violation can justify investigating the implicated path, but it does not by itself identify the architectural revision that will resolve it. Conversely, a result that supports the intended claim may justify retaining the candidate for the next evaluation without changing its design. Feedback selects among these actions; whether a finding should also change the search method is a separate learning decision.

Which of these questions dominates depends on where the system sits among the three layers of @fig-ch01-three-layers-ai-integration. An L1 (AI-Assisted) draft whose testbench came from the same model may reproduce the same omissions; an L2 (AI-Driven) optimizer scoring a floorplan on proxy wirelength can game the proxy without ever violating it. An L3 (AI-Native) system must coordinate checks across the boundaries its search can change, choosing formal, power-intent, structural, or mutation checks to cover the declared claims and expose shared blind spots. An interrupted run may still supply completed measurements or proofs, provided their lineage, completion status, and scope can be established independently of the interrupted work. Outputs whose status remains uncertain are retained without treating them as completed evidence; no partial return supports the uncompleted obligation. If a timing check omits a required PVT corner, it cannot establish timing feasibility at that corner. Likewise, a missing Unified Power Format (UPF) isolation check leaves the corresponding power-state behavior unqualified; a completed check that finds an isolation violation supplies evidence of a design or power-intent defect. Missing checks and demonstrated violations require different responses even when both prevent a broader feasibility claim.

## Evaluation Signal Sources and Signoff Attrition

The signals that qualification works on span a wide range of latency, spatial granularity, and physical fidelity. Analytical roofline estimators can evaluate simple kernels quickly, while cycle-accurate simulation and full-chip physical signoff may take hours. Hardware emulation provides another tradeoff, supporting long instruction traces at a higher execution rate than software simulation. For an illustrative scheduling comparison, suppose a roofline estimate takes under a millisecond and a physical signoff run takes 12–48\ hours; these are assumed latencies, not measurements or universal tool runtimes. Static timing, dynamic IR-drop, and design rule checking in electronic design automation (EDA) engines return different kinds of failures. An IR-drop report from RedHawk-SC may locate a violation on the die, while Cadence Tempus may identify a failing timing path.[^fn-ir-drop-c07] Those reports help diagnosis but do not by themselves establish which upstream architectural choice should change. Lineage binding the metric to candidate parameters, RTL revisions, tool flags, and constraints makes that investigation possible.

Control theory supplies a useful warning: feedback delay and noise constrain how aggressively a controller can respond [@AstromMurray2008FeedbackSystems]. Architectural search is not necessarily a continuous controller, so that warning alone does not establish its stability or latency budget. It does expose the risk of proposing many changes before their physical consequences return. One arrangement uses fast, qualified proxies to steer exploration while slower signoff results recalibrate those proxies and reopen affected candidates. The system must retain which revision each delayed result checked.

Automated verification is a structural need rather than a convenience. A design with $|S|$ Boolean state bits has at most $2^{|S|}$ possible states; the subset reachable under its reset and input assumptions can be smaller. The longitudinal Wilson Research Group surveys discussed in @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales place verification effort alongside persistent first-pass silicon failures, the *verification scissors*. Random stimulus can leave corner-case deadlocks and races unexercised, so adding vectors alone does not establish their absence. Generative proposal velocity can widen this gap unless stage-matched qualification filters the candidate pool. Published RTL-generation benchmarks report failures in syntax and functional testing [@VerilogEval; @RTLLM]. The constructed five-stage funnel in @fig-synthesis-verification-funnel illustrates how successive checks can reduce a candidate pool. Its stages are syntax parsing, interface and interconnect compliance, functional assertion checking, static timing analysis, and physical design-rule and layout-versus-schematic checks (@fig-synthesis-verification-funnel a). This is an illustrative ordering, not a universal signoff flow or a measured benchmark yield.

![**Composed stage attrition collapses candidate pools, shown as a constructed illustration.** (a) Attrition across five signoff stages as constructed per-stage pass rates compound from 100,000 proposals to fewer than 100 survivors. (b) Conditional pass rate for each stage given survival of prior stages. Published RTL-generation benchmarks report syntax and functional-test failures [@VerilogEval; @RTLLM]; the rates shown here are constructed and do not represent measured physical-signoff yields.](images/fig-synthesis-verification-funnel){#fig-synthesis-verification-funnel width="80%" fig-alt="Two-panel visualization showing candidate attrition across five physical verification signoff stages from 100,000 proposals down to fewer than 100 surviving candidates alongside stage-specific conditional pass rates. Values are constructed for illustration."}

The displayed pass rates are conditional on survival of the earlier stages (@fig-synthesis-verification-funnel b). If $N_0$ proposals enter the funnel and $p_i$ is the fraction entering stage $i$ that passes it, then $N_5 = N_0\prod_{i=1}^{5}p_i$. This multiplication does not assume independent checks: each rate describes the pool left by the preceding checks. Changing the order can change those conditional rates, so they cannot simply be carried over to a reordered funnel.

In this ordering, rejecting a malformed proposal at parsing avoids spending resources on the later checks. Early filtering can therefore make a larger proposal stream affordable, provided the filter itself is suitable for the candidates it screens. To choose an order, consider what each check can reject, how long it takes, which artifacts it requires, and how much later work a justified rejection avoids. A cheap check belongs early when its result can support that rejection; passing it leaves the obligations addressed by later checks open. Every empirical observation entering the search loop also needs admission criteria before it is compared with anything.

## Empirical Admission Criteria

An empirical measurement needs enough context to establish what was measured before it can enter a comparison. A clean exit code may hide uninitialized cache warmup states (where cold-start misses distort instructions per cycle), uncalibrated process corners, or truncated trace intervals. The seven record elements in @tbl-measurement-record make these conditions inspectable. Together they identify the value, establish how it was extracted, and state the variation and error that limit its use.

| **Record Element** | **Question the record must answer** |
| - | - |
| Candidate identity | Which design revision, hardware configuration, software state, and workload produced the value? |
| Quantity and unit | What architectural metric was computed, how was it aggregated, and in what unit? |
| Conditions | Which tool and model versions, random-number generator (RNG) seeds, and process, voltage, and temperature (PVT) conditions are relevant to this quantity? |
| Extraction status | Did the expected output artifact exist, parse under the declared schema, and retain raw logs? |
| Variation and error | What repetitions, sampling methods, numerical tolerances, or error bounds restrict the value? |
| Constraint integrity | Which versions of applicable timing constraints in Synopsys Design Constraints (SDC) form, power intent (UPF), and waiver manifests were used, and how are they identified, for example by recorded SHA-256 hashes? |
| Source record | Which returned artifact, extraction procedure, and execution record support this metric, and what dependencies would be needed to reproduce it? |
: **A measurement requires identity, meaning, conditions, and limits.** These record elements establish whether a measurement is eligible for a scoped comparison; the comparison itself needs additional qualification. {#tbl-measurement-record tbl-colwidths="[28,72]"}

Passing admission criteria qualifies a metric as eligible for comparison, but does not validate the comparison itself. That judgment requires evaluating the complete experimental delta under matched operating conditions, as developed in @sec-evidence-specific-to-claim-and-scope. Before comparing candidates, however, we need to distinguish a measured quantity from a different kind of return: a proof that a candidate obeys a required contract. A cache's measured latency and a proof that its controller preserves transaction ordering answer different questions, even when both arrive through the same execution interface.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="A returned value must qualify before it becomes feedback"}
**Context.** Consider a hypothetical return from evaluating a prospective L2 cache configuration for the Lighthouse XR subsystem under a 3\ W thermal design power (TDP) envelope. Suppose static UPF checks pass, but a bounded model checking (BMC) run encounters a setup failure, and a thermal report omits raw trace lineage. These statuses illustrate routing; the Lighthouse study has not executed.

**Application.** For the thermal value, the required context includes the activity trace, power and thermal models, applicable operating conditions, and extraction procedure. Hardware and software revisions, the instruction set architecture (ISA), compiler state, and memory timing assumptions must also be identified where they affect that activity or its interpretation. The missing raw trace lineage prevents this value from entering a comparison; unrelated completed checks retain their own scope. Passing static UPF checks neither supplies that lineage nor resolves the BMC setup failure.

**Outcome.** The setup failure routes to environment repair, and the incomplete thermal value remains unqualified. Neither return establishes a defect in the architectural candidate. Retaining that distinction prevents infrastructure failures from becoming false negative training labels.
:::

## Formal Bounds and Sequential Equivalence {#sec-formal-bounds-sequential-equivalence}

A comparative performance claim needs a matched baseline; a safety property can be checked directly against its declared model and assumptions. While dynamic simulation exercises sampled execution traces, a completed unbounded formal proof establishes that an implementation satisfies an invariant across all reachable states within those assumptions. In automated exploration loops, such proofs can establish interface protocol compliance, rule out specified control hazards, or certify equivalence before expensive downstream synthesis and place-and-route runs. A bounded search or an inconclusive run supports a narrower conclusion, so the returned proof status matters as much as the property itself.

### Proof Statuses and Contract Equivalence

Properties (expressed as SystemVerilog Assertions (SVA) for formal temporal logic proofs) specify microarchitectural contracts, while assumptions in formal tools (JasperGold, VC Formal) constrain legal input sequences, resets, and clock domains [@Clarke2018ModelChecking]. When verifying simplified abstract models, counterexample-guided abstraction refinement (CEGAR) evaluates returned failure traces against the concrete RTL: *spurious counterexamples* (artifacts of over-approximated abstraction that cannot occur in real hardware) trigger automatic model refinement, whereas *realizable counterexamples* expose genuine RTL bugs or specification errors [@ClarkeEtAl2000CEGAR].[^fn-cegar-c07]

Beyond property checking on individual blocks, completed formal proofs can establish behavioral equivalence across representations. *Combinational equivalence checking* (CEC) compares logic between aligned state elements to check whether logic synthesis preserves gate-level truth tables. *Sequential equivalence checking* (SEC) checks behavioral correspondence for microarchitectural transformations that alter pipeline register boundaries, retiming stages, or transaction latencies, subject to the correspondence defined for the check [@Kropf1999FormalVerification]. At system interfaces, *assume-guarantee reasoning* modularly verifies block contracts: for example, a proof can establish that if a bus fabric satisfies transaction ordering assumptions, the connected accelerator guarantees credit-queue safety [@BenvenisteEtAl2018Contracts].

Equivalence checks define what counts as 'the same behavior,' but this definition must follow the architectural claim. CEC compares corresponding combinational functions under an agreed state correspondence. SEC additionally reasons about behavior over time; permitted retiming or latency correspondence must be part of the checking setup.

An exact-reference comparison may reject a candidate that changes interface timing, lengthens a tolerated latency, or changes ordering within what the specification permits. That mismatch can be correct for the selected reference even when the new behavior is legal. Replacing the reference with the candidate itself would evade the question rather than resolve it.

The relevant obligation is then refinement: every implementation behavior must correspond to a behavior allowed by the specification. A *refinement mapping* relates the implementation's state to the specification's state so that this correspondence can be proved [@AbadiLamport1991RefinementMappings]. The check must declare the permitted latency shifts and protocol changes in advance. A log reporting 'equivalence passed' supports only the reference and correspondence that were actually checked.

### Bounded Search and Vacuity

Bounded model checking (BMC) unrolls transition relations to depth $k$ to catch shallow defects [@BiereEtAl1999BMC]. Finding no counterexample through $k$ supports a bounded claim. To establish unbounded safety, the checker must additionally establish that this depth is sufficient to cover every reachable violation, or complete a separate proof using $k$-induction or property-directed reachability (IC3/PDR) [@Bradley2011IC3; @EenEtAl2011PDR]. Increasing $k$ alone does not supply that completeness argument.

Deeper unrolling explores longer behaviors but can exhaust the solver budget (@fig-sva-bmc-coverage-depth). In the constructed illustration, shallow control structures (such as direct memory access [DMA] ring-buffer controllers) reach a complete proof at moderate depths, conditional on establishing completeness or a separate inductive proof. Complex state machines (such as multi-tile systolic array controllers) instead encounter state-space explosion and Boolean satisfiability (SAT) solver timeouts. The depths at which either happens depend on the specific design and solver; the curves are not a way to infer a proof status from depth alone.

![**Formal coverage and solver runtime versus BMC depth, a constructed illustration.** The left axis conceptually depicts coverage rising with BMC depth $k$ across four accelerator units. Complete-proof endpoints for shallow control units (DMA controllers and barrier synchronizers) assume an established completeness threshold or a separate inductive proof; depth alone establishes only a bounded result. Complex multi-tile systolic controllers and arbiters encounter state-space explosion and SAT solver timeout barriers. The right axis (log scale) shows exponential growth in solver runtime. Curves are constructed to show the characteristic shape; they are not measurements from any model-checking run.](images/fig-sva-bmc-coverage-depth){#fig-sva-bmc-coverage-depth width="80%" fig-alt="Dual-axis plot showing SVA formal state-space coverage rising with BMC depth k across four accelerator execution units on the primary left axis alongside exponential SAT solver runtime on the secondary log-scale axis, highlighting solver timeout walls beyond depth 45."}

*Safety properties* exclude forbidden behavior (such as mutual exclusion violations), while *liveness properties* require eventual progress, often under explicit fairness assumptions [@AlpernSchneider1985Liveness]. Both are trace properties: membership is determined for one execution at a time, although a liveness violation may require an infinite trace. Noninterference relates executions that differ in a secret and asks whether an unprivileged observer can distinguish them. It is a *hyperproperty[^fn-hyper-c07]*, a property of a set of traces [@ClarksonSchneider2010Hyperproperties]. The paired-execution check used for this form of noninterference cannot be replaced by inspecting one execution in isolation; hyperproperties in general are not limited to pairs. SPECTECTOR checks speculative noninterference through symbolic execution under declared speculative semantics, comparing observations with and without speculation [@GuarnieriEtAl2020SPECTECTOR]. The property class therefore determines the checking problem before depth and budget are chosen.

Vacuity checks ask whether an assertion succeeds without exercising the behavior it was intended to constrain [@BeerEtAl2001Vacuity]. For example, an assertion that every accepted request eventually receives a response can pass vacuously if the environment assumptions prevent any request from being accepted. A cover query for request acceptance under the same assumptions tests whether that trigger is reachable. A witness rules out this particular source of vacuity; it does not prove the response obligation. If the cover query establishes that acceptance is unreachable, inspect the assumptions and trigger before using the assertion to support a progress claim. A bounded search without a witness leaves reachability beyond that bound unresolved.

Automated assertion generators (e.g., AssertLLM) require syntactic and semantic qualification, including seeded-mutant checks of whether their proposed assertions detect relevant defects [@FangEtAl2025AssertLLM; @PulavarthiEtAl2025AssertionGeneration]. Mutation testing adds a different question: does the assertion detect an introduced defect? Trigger reachability alone does not establish that sensitivity; @sec-semantic-rtl-defects develops how to assess it.

One route from bounded checking to an unbounded safety proof is $k$-induction. In the following indexing convention, the *base query* $B_k$ searches for a property violation from the initial state through step $k$. The *inductive-step query* $S_k$ searches for a transition from states $s_0$ through $s_k$ that satisfy the property to a state $s_{k+1}$ that violates it:

$$B_k = \bigvee_{j=0}^{k}\left(Init(s_0) \land \bigwedge_{i=0}^{j-1} T(s_i,s_{i+1}) \land \neg P(s_j)\right),$$

$$S_k = \bigwedge_{i=0}^{k} P(s_i) \land \bigwedge_{i=0}^{k} T(s_i,s_{i+1}) \land \neg P(s_{k+1}),$$

where $Init(s_0)$ constrains the initial state, $T(s_i, s_{i+1})$ is the hardware transition relation, and $P(s)$ is the target safety invariant. The base query considers every prefix length from zero through $k$, including traces that cannot continue; the empty transition conjunction at $j=0$ is true. If $B_k$ is unsatisfiable, no violation is reachable from $Init$ through step $k$; $Init$ must encode any reset assumptions the claim requires. If $S_k$ is unsatisfiable, every trajectory satisfying $P$ in the $k+1$ consecutive states $s_0,\ldots,s_k$ also satisfies it in the next state. Unsatisfiability of both queries establishes unbounded safety for this induction construction. A satisfiable base query instead supplies a reachable counterexample.

The inductive-step query does not require its starting state to be reachable from $Init$. A satisfying trace may therefore begin in an unreachable state, producing a *spurious inductive counterexample* rather than a hardware bug. The verifier can increase the induction depth or seek auxiliary invariants $Inv(s)$ that strengthen the property. The proof must establish the strengthened condition $P(s) \land Inv(s)$ from $Init$ and show that it is preserved by the modeled transitions. Simply assuming an auxiliary condition could exclude a real defect. Property-directed reachability (PDR / IC3) takes another route, maintaining over-approximated reachability frames $F_0, F_1, \dots, F_k$ and learning clauses that block unreachable counterexamples until it finds a suitable inductive invariant or a reachable violation [@Bradley2011IC3; @EenEtAl2011PDR].

Formal verification statuses dictate distinct downstream engineering actions (@tbl-formal-result-status).

| **Formal status** | **What it establishes** | **Eligible next action** |
| - | - | - |
| **Proved** | Property holds for recorded model and assumptions under verified checking components. | Discharge the scoped architectural claim once the property and assumptions are qualified, including relevant vacuity checks. |
| **Counterexample** | A trace satisfies the violation query; its reachability and realizability depend on the query and abstraction. | Check reachability and realizability. Refine a spurious abstraction, strengthen a failed induction argument with proved invariants, or repair RTL or specification for a confirmed failure. |
| **Bounded-only** | No counterexample found through depth $k$. | Record finite bound; extend search, seek a completeness argument or separate proof, or leave unbounded safety open. |
| **Inconclusive** | Solver timed out or exceeded memory limits. | Revise abstraction, decompose assumptions, or adjust resource bounds. Never report as a pass. |
: **Formal result status dictates next technical actions in verification feedback.** Proofs discharge scoped claims; counterexamples and bounds drive targeted repairs or open records. {#tbl-formal-result-status tbl-colwidths="[20,40,40]"}

An inconclusive status establishes neither a proof nor a violation. The tool may still retain a checked bound or another partial result, which needs its own qualification. A clean process exit cannot substitute for the declared property status. Bounded-only carries a different hazard: it is evidence through depth $k$, but the depth must travel with the result or the claim quietly becomes an unbounded one.

## Dynamic Coverage and Mutation Testing {#sec-semantic-rtl-defects}

A proof covers what its property set, model, and assumptions name (@sec-formal-bounds-sequential-equivalence). Other claims still need suitable checks. Full system-on-chip (SoC) software workloads and dynamic thermal behavior pose modeling and scale challenges for formal analysis, while cycle-accurate simulation and hardware emulation exercise long execution traces without covering every corner case. Verification suites therefore combine methods, using formal proofs for selected interface protocols, arbiters, and crossing properties, and dynamic evaluation for workload throughput, power, and end-to-end latency under the modeled conditions.

Dynamic verification pairs constrained-random simulation (Synopsys VCS, Verilator) and Universal Verification Methodology (UVM) coverage metrics [@IEEE2020UVM; @IEEE2023SystemVerilog] with hardware emulation platforms (Palladium, ZeBu, Veloce). Low-power verification combines static Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE) 1801 UPF power-state tables (PSTs) with low-power-aware simulation to verify power isolation clamping cells and level shifters across power domains [@IEEE2024UPF]. A power estimate also needs the applicable power-state transitions qualified; an RTL simulation that omits those transitions leaves their effects untested. Sampled dynamic simulation cannot prove the absence of rare corner-case bugs, as demonstrated by the historic Pentium floating-point division (FDIV) lookup table defect [@SharangpaniBarton1994FDIV; @Edelman1997PentiumDivision; @Colwell2006PentiumChronicles].

::: {.callout-case-study title="The Pentium FDIV flaw and the limit of sampled testing"}
**Context:** Pre-silicon execution-unit verification passed millions of random division vectors.

**Defect:** Five omitted entries out of 1,066 in the radix-4 SRT division programmable logic array (PLA) manifested only once in 9 billion random divisions [@SharangpaniBarton1994FDIV; @Edelman1997PentiumDivision].

**Outcome:** Sampled dynamic simulation cannot guarantee defect absence in high-dimensional state spaces. A later industrial example of addressing this limitation is the use of formal verification in Intel Core i7 execution-engine validation [@KaivolaEtAl2009Corei7Formal].
:::

Sampled stimulus is one limit of dynamic coverage. The other is the checker. A testbench drafted alongside the RTL can execute defective logic without detecting the wrong outcome, especially if both inherit an omitted requirement. Syntactic validity leaves semantic and physical questions open, including clock and reset crossings, interface ordering, and power-domain isolation. The following eight examples show which checks can address those questions; they are not an empirical ranking of the defects in generated RTL.

1. **Inferred latches and combinational loops.** An incomplete assignment in intended combinational logic can imply state retention, producing a latch inference or a tool diagnostic. A selected stimulus may miss the unintended behavior, and the latch introduces timing obligations such as hold checks.[^fn-hold-timing-c07] Lint and synthesis reports expose unintended storage and combinational feedback; functional tests establish only the behaviors they exercise.
2. **Clock-domain crossing (CDC) and reset-domain crossing (RDC) metastability.** An asynchronous input that changes near a receiving clock edge can leave a flip-flop metastable, with a risk that its output does not settle before downstream logic samples it. Synchronization must fit the transfer: a dual-rank synchronizer can reduce the risk for a suitable single-bit control signal, while a multi-bit transfer needs a protocol that preserves coherence, such as a properly designed asynchronous first-in, first-out (FIFO). Reset deassertion that violates recovery or removal timing can similarly leave state elements inconsistent. Ordinary RTL simulation does not model the analog settling process. Dedicated CDC and RDC analysis checks crossing structures, protocols, and assumptions, with formal or metastability-injection checks where appropriate.
3. **Interface handshake and memory-ordering violations.** An Advanced eXtensible Interface (AXI) source that waits for `READY` before asserting `VALID` can deadlock with a receiver waiting for `VALID`; dropping an unacknowledged transfer can lose data. A testbench whose receiver never stalls may miss both defects. Separately, generated logic or software that assumes sequential consistency can fail under behaviors permitted by RISC-V Weak Memory Ordering (RVWMO). The relevant tests must exercise those behaviors and compare them with the declared memory model; a core count alone does not determine that coverage. Interface assertions and assume-guarantee proofs can check the handshake obligations, while memory-model tests or proofs check the ordering assumptions.
4. **Bitwidth truncation and overflow.** A vector accumulator that silently drops precision can pass stimulus that never reaches the affected range. Width lint flags potential truncation; directed boundary-value tests or formal checks establish whether the implemented wraparound or saturation matches the specification.
5. **Unhandled reset states in finite state machines (FSMs).** An FSM lacking a recovery transition from an unused encoding can become stuck if a fault or unexpected control sequence places it there. FSM lint and reachability analysis help identify missing behavior; a fault-injection claim also needs a model of how the fault enters the state. Simulation detects the problem only when its stimulus and fault model exercise it.
6. **Four-state $1\text{'bx}$ optimism.** Under ordinary IEEE 1800 semantics, `if (1'bx)` takes the `else` branch [@IEEE2023SystemVerilog]. That choice can hide uncertainty about an uninitialized or otherwise unknown control value. X is a simulation value, not a particular physical voltage: the corresponding hardware may hold either logic value, or the model may be abstracting a different electrical problem.[^fn-x-optimism-c07] X-propagation-aware simulation and formal checks that account for unknown initial state can expose behaviors masked by the ordinary branch semantics. Their unknown-value assumptions remain part of the check.
7. **Missing isolation and level shifting across power domains.** Required level shifting depends on the voltage compatibility of the crossing; required isolation depends on power states and the receiving interface's needs [@IEEE2024UPF]. Omitting required isolation can feed an invalid logic level into an active domain. In a simplified CMOS inverter, an input in the range $V_{tn} < V_{in} < V_{dd} - |V_{tp}|$ can turn on both transistor networks and draw crowbar current. Static UPF checks and low-power-aware simulation address the declared structure and modeled behavior; they do not quantify all electrical consequences, including latchup risk.[^fn-latchup-c07] Those require suitable device and power-network analysis.
8. **Silent false paths and multicycle overrides in SDC constraints.** An optimizer can hide a real timing violation by inserting an unjustified `set_false_path` or `set_multicycle_path` directive. A clean report then leaves the underlying path unchecked or checked against an inappropriate requirement. Independent constraint review and SDC lint can challenge the exception; the timing report alone cannot, because the engine follows the supplied constraints. The 850\ ps instance in @sec-timing-exception-attacks illustrates a reported absence of negative slack despite a real setup failure.

Using the same large language model (LLM) family to generate RTL and its testbench risks reproducing the same omissions, a *self-verification paradox*. Mutation testing challenges the suite by introducing faults such as inverted branches or stuck-at bits and measuring which non-equivalent mutants it detects.[^fn-red-teaming-c07] Structural coverage records which code or transitions were exercised; mutant detection tests whether the suite notices particular wrong outcomes. Mutation-based RISC-V compliance testing supplies a published example of using surviving mutants to guide additional tests [@HerdtEtAl2021MutationCompliance]. The four-tier quantitative exhibit in @fig-testbench-vacuity has unverified provenance and is not evidence of an AI-testbench result or a measured comparison among those tiers.

![**Structural coverage and fault detection are different quantities; this exhibit's quantitative provenance is unverified.** The displayed values label directed tests with $88.4\%$ line coverage and $34.8\%$ mutant detection, a $53.6$ point difference, and label constrained-random UVM, compliance tests, and formal/symbolic checking with $58.6\%$, $91.8\%$, and $100\%$ detection. The associated count of $1{,}240$ non-equivalent mutants and the common basis for comparing these tiers have not been verified against a source or retained experiment. These values therefore support no empirical ranking or coverage-gap estimate.](images/fig-testbench-vacuity){#fig-testbench-vacuity width="80%" fig-alt="Grouped bar chart with unverified quantitative provenance comparing line coverage and mutant detection across four labeled verification tiers. The displayed 53.6-point gap and tier rankings must not be interpreted as verified empirical results."}

Adding simulation cycles can yield diminishing returns when the remaining faults require narrowly targeted stimulus. The constructed survival model in @fig-mutation-roi illustrates that possibility: early faults are found quickly, while a small population survives continued randomized testing. A surviving mutant gives the verification team a more specific question than low coverage alone does. Which state transition would expose this fault, and which assertion would notice the resulting error?

One proposed use of agents is to automate that investigation through *agentic mutation testing*. Mutation Cover with Yosys modifies signals in a synthesized netlist to create mutants. Non-equivalent mutants are identified, and the simulation suite runs against them. For a surviving mutant, the environment could return the mutation details and available source locations to an agent that proposes a SystemVerilog Assertion (SVA) or a directed testbench sequence. The suite must then run again to establish whether the new check detects the fault while accepting the correct design. Killing the retained mutants supports a claim about detection of that tested fault set. It does not establish that all corner cases have been found, that the original specification is complete, or that the agent and checker have no shared omissions.

![**Diminishing returns in a constructed mutation-survival model.** The illustrative series decreases from near $100\%$ survival toward an assumed floor near $5\%$ across $20{,}000$ simulation compute hours. The local dataset identifies these values as a stylized analytical model, not a measured testing run; no empirical fit or calibration has been established. The curve motivates targeted investigation of surviving faults without estimating a real verification budget, a universal survival floor, or the effectiveness of an agentic testing system.](images/plot_ch7.png){#fig-mutation-roi width="80%" fig-alt="Constructed line graph of mutant survival declining toward an assumed floor near 5 percent across 20,000 simulation compute hours. The series is illustrative and has no established empirical calibration."}

An evaluator drawn from the generator's own model family may repeat the same omissions. Such a second opinion can corroborate an answer without independently challenging it, the distinction developed in @fig-independent-checks and treated as a red-team target in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect. A design environment therefore needs fault-detection measurements alongside structural coverage, and claim-specific checks whose assumptions remain visible. Formal proof engines supply one such check for declared properties; their proofs still depend on the specification they are given.

## Scoping a Comparison to the Claim It Supports {#sec-evidence-specific-to-claim-and-scope}

A correctness proof or a qualified functional testbench does not by itself rank two candidates by performance. Once individual measurements meet the admission criteria, an empirical claim that one design outperforms a baseline still needs an evaluation that separates the hardware effect from confounding variation under matched workloads. That comparison requires control over compiler lowering, memory initial states, simulator versions, and operating corners. An isolated delta cannot distinguish a hardware gain from simulation jitter, cold-start cache artifacts, or compiler phase-ordering shifts without those controls.

Every comparison binds candidate and comparator revisions to a measured difference and uncertainty model under explicit operating conditions (@fig-claim-frame).

![**Comparative claim frames bind candidate and baseline designs to measured deltas.** Compared designs (candidate and comparator) map to measured results (quantities, units, differences, and uncertainty). These remain conditional on experimental scope (workloads, architectural state, tool versions, PVT corners, and check nonclaims). A change in evaluation scope creates a distinct comparison rather than an interchangeable measurement.](images/fig-claim-frame){#fig-claim-frame width="80%" fig-alt="Three-column comparison frame. Candidate and comparator feed a measured quantity, difference, and uncertainty. These are bounded by workload and design state, tool conditions, and check scope."}

For a matched set of architectural evaluation cases $c_j \in \mathcal{C}$ (representing identical benchmark inputs, initial cache states, and PVT operating corners), the paired difference is:

$$
d_j = y(\text{candidate}, c_j) - y(\text{comparator}, c_j),
$$

where $y(\cdot)$ denotes the evaluated architectural metric. For positive per-benchmark performance ratios, a geometric mean preserves comparisons when the normalization reference changes, provided the benchmark set and weights remain fixed [@FlemingWallace1986HowNotToLie]. If the claim concerns total execution time for a specified workload mix, aggregate execution times using that mix before forming a ratio.

Confounding factors (simulator versions, compiler flags, thermal states, and cache warmup intervals) can create apparent performance deltas independent of architectural interventions [@GutierrezEtAl2014SourcesOfError; @PeherstorferWillcoxGunzburger2018Multifidelity]. For paired observations with temporal dependence, block resampling estimates uncertainty while preserving local dependence within sampled blocks [@Kunsch1989BlockBootstrap]. The block choice and sampling assumptions remain part of the interval's qualification. A comparison also needs a decision margin $m$, the smallest difference in $y$ that would change the architectural decision, declared before measurement. An interval crossing zero leaves the direction unresolved. An interval wholly inside $\pm m$ supports the narrower conclusion that the difference is below the declared practical margin, even if its direction is unresolved. This difference-below-decision-margin status is retained under @tbl-feedback-destinations without forcing a design update.

A decision-relevant improvement needs evidence relative to $m$ in the metric's favorable direction. With candidate-minus-comparator differences, an interval wholly below $-m$ supports such an improvement for a lower-is-better metric such as latency; an interval wholly above $m$ does so for a higher-is-better metric such as throughput. An interval that excludes zero but crosses the favorable decision threshold supports a direction without resolving whether the gain is large enough to change the decision. Further measurement is justified when resolving that uncertainty could change the choice; otherwise, the comparison can be retained with its limit explicit.

Selecting the top performer among thousands of noisy evaluations adds a second hazard, the selection bias that @sec-support-limits introduced as the optimizer's curse. The estimates used to select a winner tend to overstate its advantage. The apparent margin therefore needs an independent confirmatory measurement before it supports an improvement claim.

::: {.callout-law title="The Winner's Curse in Multi-Agent Tournaments"}
**The Classical Principle:** Selection among noisy estimates can favor optimistic error. The winner's curse names this hazard in competitive bidding [@CapenEtAl1971CompetitiveBidding; @Thaler1988WinnersCurse]; the optimizer's curse applies the selection argument more generally. For a fixed finite candidate set, let $v_i$ be candidate $i$'s true value, with larger values preferred, and let $\hat v_i$ be an unbiased estimate. Selecting $I=\arg\max_i\hat v_i$ gives $\mathbb{E}[\hat v_I-v_I]\geq0$, with expectation over repeated evaluations [@SmithWinkler2006OptimizersCurse]. The inequality is strict if noise can cause selection of a candidate whose true value is below the optimum. This is an average selection effect, not a guarantee that every winning estimate is too high or has the largest measurement error.

**The Hardware Trap:** A sweep can select a microarchitecture partly because a sampled workload phase or random tool variation favored it. A deterministic simulator omission is a separate hazard: repeated runs with the same model can reproduce the same misleading advantage.

**The Architectural Antidote:** Confirm the selected design on fresh seeds where randomness matters and on held-out workload phases. Challenge suspected model omissions with a check that can observe them; reseeding the same simulator is insufficient (@sec-law-winners-curse in @sec-appendix-b-laws-paradoxes).
:::

## Qualifying Proxies and Calibration {#sec-proxy-mismatch-metric-gaming-and-calibration}

Independent confirmatory evaluation tests a selected candidate, but exploration also needs faster ways to decide which candidates to test. Analytical cost models, cycle-approximate simulators, and learned surrogates serve that role. When a surrogate diverges from physical behavior, search can exploit modeling omissions such as ignored dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) bank serialization, interconnect contention, or thermal dissipation limits. This is microarchitectural proxy gaming (@sec-architecture-20-ontology) [@Goodhart1975MonetaryManagement; @Strathern1997Goodhart]. A better surrogate score then need not yield a better implementable design. Qualifying the proxy requires separating *observed qualification strata*, regions represented by paired proxy and reference measurements, from *unsampled evaluation gaps* (@fig-trust-calibration) [@WunderlichEtAl2003SMARTS; @SherwoodEtAl2002SimPoint; @ForresterSobesterKeane2008Surrogate].

![**Discrete qualification strata expose unsampled proxy evaluation gaps, shown conceptually.** Paired proxy and reference observations anchor confidence only at discrete sampled strata (Q1, Q2, Q3). Unsampled gaps between strata, and regions beyond the sampled support, risk severe divergence between surrogate scores and stronger reference evaluations [@WunderlichEtAl2003SMARTS; @SherwoodEtAl2002SimPoint; @ForresterSobesterKeane2008Surrogate]. Curves are conceptual representations of search progression versus normalized objective value, not measured data points.](images/fig-trust-calibration){#fig-trust-calibration width="80%" fig-alt="Conceptual normalized plot with three separate green qualification strata in the left-hand range. Paired proxy and stronger-reference markers appear in each stratum, while a dashed white band marks an unsampled gap between the first two. The curves may diverge as search continues into an unqualified right-hand range. No plotted curve is measured data."}

When search enters an unsampled gap, the existing observations may no longer justify the surrogate's reported error bounds, even if those bounds remain narrow. Matched reference measurements in the new region test whether rankings remain useful. Without that qualification, a candidate that looks attractive to the proxy may fail physical closure; a confident score does not settle the question.

The verification loop must therefore audit the proxy itself. Evaluating its fitness for use pairs specific failure modes with diagnostic checks (@tbl-proxy-diagnostics). Comparisons across performance, power, and area also need an explicit decision rule. Pareto dominance identifies when one candidate is at least as good in every objective and better in at least one; a scalar objective instead encodes particular preferences or tradeoffs, which must be declared [@Deb2001MultiObjective].

| **Concern** | **Diagnostic check** | **What an adverse result means** |
| - | - | - |
| **Proxy mismatch** | Compare proxy with stronger reference measurement on matched cases against the tolerance required for the intended use. | Disagreement beyond that tolerance leaves the intended use unsupported; other uses require separate checks. |
| **Observed coverage** | Map candidate and tool dimensions; identify unsampled gaps. | Evidence does not qualify candidates outside sampled strata. |
| **Held-out agreement** | Measure error and ranking stability against decision margins on held-out cases. | Excessive error limits quantitative estimates; unstable rankings limit ordering for the declared use, even within observed strata. |
| **Confounding** | Hold versions and budgets fixed using matched contrasts. | Measured difference does not identify proposed architectural cause. |
| **Variability** | Repeat stochastic flows and report dispersion. | If uncertainty prevents resolving the declared decision margin, the point estimate alone cannot justify the decision. |
| **Selection bias** | Re-evaluate selected candidate on fresh, unseen cases. | Original apparent margin is not independently confirmed. |
: **Each weakness requires a distinct diagnostic.** Adverse results eliminate specific inferences without making other diagnoses interchangeable. {#tbl-proxy-diagnostics tbl-colwidths="[24,38,38]"}

The third column limits what the architect can infer from each diagnostic. Failure on one task need not make the surrogate useless for every other task, but another use still needs its own qualification. A proxy unreliable for fine ranking might support coarse screening only if its false-acceptance and false-rejection behavior is acceptable for that screen. Passing the observed checks also does not establish behavior outside their qualified scope.

## Outcome, Mechanism, and Counterfactual Reasoning

A proxy qualified for a particular use in @sec-proxy-mismatch-metric-gaming-and-calibration does not by itself explain why a candidate performs better. An observed top-line *outcome* and its proposed explanatory *mechanism* require separate judgments (@tbl-outcome-mechanism). When an automated optimizer modifies a microarchitectural feature, recording an improvement in top-line latency or throughput does not prove that the intended mechanism produced the gain. For instance, a cache resizing candidate might post improved frame rendering times not because larger static random-access memory (SRAM) capacity reduced conflict misses, but because incidental compiler instruction alignment masked a memory bus serialization stall. Establishing architectural causality requires counterfactual testing through controlled contrast experiments that hold confounding compiler, memory, and operating variables fixed while probing the isolated mechanism.

| **Evaluation question** | **Possible qualified status** | **Why the distinction matters** |
| - | - | - |
| **Did requested quantity change in declared direction?** | Supported, contradicted, or unresolved. | Latency confidence interval spanning zero leaves improvement unresolved. |
| **Did proposed intermediate effect occur?** | Supported, contradicted, unresolved, or untested. | Qualified reduction in capacity misses confirms bounded cache effect. |
| **Did intermediate effect cause the outcome?** | Supported only by distinguishing contrast under identification assumptions. | Lower miss count alone does not prove it caused tail-latency reduction. |
| **What did the check fundamentally not observe?** | Explicit nonclaims. | Cache-local results do not establish thermal stability or functional correctness. |
: **Outcome and mechanism remain separate results.** Intermediate effects cannot substitute for unresolved architectural comparisons. {#tbl-outcome-mechanism tbl-colwidths="[34,30,36]"}

Generated explanations need the same scrutiny. A fluent causal narrative about a candidate's success is a hypothesis until measurements test it. Useful observations include performance-counter deltas, cycle-accurate stall breakdowns, queue-occupancy profiles, and ablation traces in which the mechanism is switched off and the outcome remeasured.

To distinguish the two explanations above, compare the original and enlarged cache at each of two controlled instruction alignments, using the same workload and holding the remaining compiler, memory, and operating settings fixed. If changing alignment reproduces the gain while adding capacity at fixed alignment yields no resolved benefit, the contrast would challenge the capacity explanation. A gain from added capacity at both alignments would support a capacity contribution. Both factors may contribute: an alignment benefit does not by itself rule out a capacity benefit. Miss counts and bus-stall breakdowns would then help test the proposed path from capacity through fewer misses to lower latency. If the capacity effect depends on alignment, retain that interaction in the explanation rather than attributing the gain to capacity alone. These contrasts support causal interpretation only insofar as the intervention changes the intended factor and the relevant conditions remain matched.

The prospective Lighthouse L2 cache configuration shows what the test has to separate. A larger L2 might reduce off-chip DRAM traffic enough to improve 99th-percentile frame latency. Evaluating that benefit also requires counting added SRAM area, leakage, tag-array lookup delay, and network-on-chip (NoC) queue pressure. The same capacity increase that raises the hit rate can lengthen the tag lookup or serialize NoC packets and make tail latency worse. Queue-occupancy profiles and latency distributions would help distinguish the capacity benefit from that failure; a hit-rate delta alone cannot.

These are trade-off hypotheses rather than measured results. The telemetry also needs checks for simulator artifacts, including a fixed-latency queueing model, omitted DRAM refresh cycles, or an unconstrained register-file assumption in the compiler backend. Each can produce an apparent mechanism that exists only in the model. A mechanism supported by the distinguishing contrast and those model checks remains qualified by the identification assumptions and the model's scope. Otherwise, it remains contradicted, unresolved, or untested according to the evidence in @tbl-outcome-mechanism; a supported outcome can still be retained separately.

## Verification and Falsification Boundaries {#sec-independent-checks-and-correlated-errors}

Qualifying individual results leaves a further question: do those results cover the requirements of the design? Assurance engineering structures this argument by linking high-level performance and correctness claims to supporting checks and explicit assumptions [@Kelly2004GSN]. For each requirement, identify the relevant checks, the conditions under which their results apply, and any remaining gap.

A successful check supports only the obligations it addresses. A check that could falsify a claim is useful even when passing it cannot establish the claim in full. Across physical limits, functional contracts, and quality-of-service bounds, the task is to determine how the checks fit together and where further evidence is needed. The following subsections develop that argument through requirement mapping, check fidelity, and shared blind spots.
### Mapping Requirements to Verification Toolchains

A complex compute subsystem needs checks matched to each physical requirement. Static timing engines such as Cadence Tempus check setup and hold timing across specified modes and corners [@Cadence2021Tempus]. Power-integrity analysis such as RedHawk-SC addresses voltage drop and electromigration limits,[^fn-em-c07] while physical verification such as Calibre checks layout against the applicable rule deck. The limiting conditions differ by property: a corner that stresses setup timing need not be the limiting corner for hold timing or leakage, and dynamic IR-drop also depends on switching activity. The verification plan must therefore name the relevant PVT conditions, activity assumptions, extraction models, and rules for each check. A pass covers those declared conditions; a nominal point estimate or a functional testbench does not establish physical feasibility across them.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="Architectural requirements remain unresolved for distinct structural reasons"}
**Context.** The prospective Lighthouse compute subsystem requirements span physical constraints, performance service-level agreements (SLAs), and correctness invariants.

**Application.** Physical limits require suitable analysis under explicit corners; performance claims need matched workload measurements with quantified uncertainty. A formal proof can discharge a named correctness invariant under its model and assumptions, while other functional requirements may need simulation, tests, or additional properties. RedHawk-SC can supply power-integrity analysis; a thermal-analysis path must be separately selected and bound before making a thermal claim.

**Outcome.** A requirement remains open if its returned check is unqualified or no check has been assigned to it. For an unqualified return, investigate the qualification gap and repair or rerun the check as needed. Where no check exists, assign a suitable evaluation path. This mapping states what the prospective subsystem would need; it does not report completed Lighthouse verification.
:::

### Scoping Observations and Check Fidelity

Every tool check in an architecture flow operates within the observational horizon @sec-data-representations-world-models records for its source, and qualification is where that horizon becomes a limit on the claim. A syntax linter verifies port lists and grammar without ensuring that logic will synthesize cleanly; a cycle-level simulator measures instruction throughput across modeled queues while remaining blind to physical layout congestion, clock-tree skew, or parasitic wire $RC$ delays.[^fn-rc-delay-c07] Upstream proxy speedups or downstream physical passes cannot expand a tool's semantic coverage beyond what its underlying mathematical model observes.

Static timing analysis makes that horizon concrete. For a simplified edge-triggered, single-clock example with a combinational timing graph, let $G=(V, E)$ contain timing pins as vertices and propagation arcs as edges. The static timing analysis (STA) engine propagates arrival times through this graph under the supplied constraints and corner models. Let $T_{\text{arr}}$ measure data arrival relative to the launch-clock edge, including clock-to-Q and data-path delay, and let positive $t_{\text{skew}}$ mean that the capture clock arrives later than the launch clock. Ignoring jitter and other uncertainty terms, the setup condition is

$$
T_{\text{arr}} \le T_{\text{req}} = T_{\text{clk}} - t_{\text{setup}} + t_{\text{skew}}
$$

while the earliest arrival satisfies the hold condition $T_{\text{arr}} \ge t_{\text{hold}} + t_{\text{skew}}$, preventing newly launched data from changing the value during the capture edge's hold interval. These inequalities cover the paths and checks enabled by the model and constraints. A `set_false_path` directive excludes matching paths from the specified timing analysis; it does not establish that the physical paths meet timing or report a meaningful zero slack for them. An unjustified exception can therefore remove a real violation from the report, as in the SDC defect class of @sec-semantic-rtl-defects. The engine may be following its inputs correctly while the checking setup omits a required obligation.

The same question, what the engine's model contains, decides what every check class can support and what it cannot establish on its own (@tbl-check-scope).

| **Check class** | **What results support under declared conditions** | **What results cannot establish by themselves** |
| - | - | - |
| Syntax and interface | Adherence to schemas, grammatical rules, and port widths. | Functional correctness, performance, power, or physical feasibility. |
| Functional simulation | Execution behavior on explicit software binaries under model semantics. | Timing closure, physical cell layout, thermal stability, and unexecuted paths. |
| Hardware emulation | Long-trace execution behavior at high effective cycle counts. | Final physical timing closure, detailed routing constraints, and power dissipation. |
| Low-power static | UPF power domain intent and structural isolation rules. | Dynamic IR-drop, power-switch settling delays, and active energy consumption. |
| Formal verification | Proofs/counterexamples for explicit properties over bounded/unbounded models. | Objectives outside the property set, or behavior under violated assumptions. |
| Architectural models | Microarchitectural cycle timing for declared workloads (gem5, ChampSim). | Physical layout limits or behaviors outside validated model regions. |
| Physical analysis | Implementation and physical results under specified models: synthesis (Yosys), place-and-route (OpenROAD), STA (Tempus), power integrity (RedHawk-SC), and separately bound thermal analysis. | Missing constraints, functional intent, or unmodeled manufacturing variation. |
| Silicon telemetry | Measured behavior of fabricated parts under test conditions. | Unmeasured workloads, operating lifetimes, or uncharacterized parts. |
: **Checks are decisive only for the properties they observe.** Costlier or downstream tools do not widen property coverage. {#tbl-check-scope tbl-colwidths="[24,38,38]"}

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Stronger Claims Require Stronger Checks"}
**The principle:** Verification rigor must match the consequences and reversibility of the architectural decision.

**The application:** High-consequence decisions demand formal proofs, signoff reports, or silicon measurements rather than uncalibrated surrogate scores.
:::

Inner-loop candidate screening tolerates bounded surrogate error, while revising a shared bus protocol or freezing pinouts for tapeout demands nonsubstitutable signoff checks. Structuring verification plans across explicit consequence tiers prevents under-checking high-risk commitments while avoiding the expense of running full signoff flows on early exploratory drafts (@tbl-feedback-by-consequence).

| **Intended use of result** | **Consequence if wrong** | **Feedback plan should include** |
| - | - | - |
| Local candidate screening | Wasted simulation budget or deferred promising candidates. | Candidate identity, matched comparator, and known proxy error bounds. |
| Shared interface revision | Downstream hardware/software work inherits errors. | Regression suites, interface compatibility checks, and explicit assumptions. |
| High-consequence commitment | Multimillion-dollar respin or tapeout failure. | Signoff checks covering all material claims, decision-margin bounds, and independent verifiers. |
: **Feedback plans must follow consequence and reversibility.** Verification rigor matches the cost of error propagation. {#tbl-feedback-by-consequence tbl-colwidths="[26,34,40]"}

Consequence and reversibility help set the required rigor. A wrong screen can waste evaluation budget or discard a useful candidate; a wrong tapeout decision can incur a mask respin and a long delay. Stronger checks reduce particular risks but do not establish zero residual risk. Adding checkers helps only to the extent that they contribute relevant information, since shared assumptions can leave shared failures unobserved.

### Correlated Blind Spots and Diverse Checkers

Superficially distinct verifiers often share underlying specifications, training corpora, or simplified timing abstractions, producing correlated errors (@fig-independent-checks) [@KnightLeveson1986Multiversion; @PanicksseryEtAl2024SelfPreference].

![**Second checks add information only when changing the failure source.** The left column illustrates how a candidate producer paired with a critic sharing the same underlying model or specification produces false correlated agreement. The right column shows how introducing a claim-specific check with an independent measurement path provides a bounded challenge, reducing correlated blind spots while requiring remaining shared baseline assumptions to be explicitly recorded [@KnightLeveson1986Multiversion; @PanicksseryEtAl2024SelfPreference].](images/fig-independent-checks){#fig-independent-checks width="80%" fig-alt="Two-column diagram. A producer and critic sharing the same assumptions lead to correlated agreement. A producer and a claim-specific check with a different measurement path lead to a bounded challenge, with remaining shared assumptions explicitly retained."}

To expose shared blind spots between superficially distinct checkers, verification suites deploy adversarial mutation testing [@DeMilloLiptonSayward1978Hints]. When a non-equivalent injected RTL defect escapes both an automated formal assertion suite and a dynamic testbench, the joint escape demonstrates a shared detection gap for that fault. The cause still needs diagnosis: both checks may inherit a specification omission, or each may miss the fault for a different reason. Furthermore, dynamic simulation and fuzzing frameworks must enforce *stimulus sensitivity* [@ZhuEtAl2025AgenticBenchmarks]. Test vectors that execute without exercising internal state transitions (such as testing an arithmetic pipeline with operand streams that never trigger carry generation, overflow saturation, or Advanced eXtensible Interface (AXI) backpressure valid-ready stalls) create a false impression of high verification pass rates while leaving physical defects dormant.

Security properties expose another shared blind spot. Spectre and Meltdown demonstrated leakage through transient execution and microarchitectural side channels that ordinary checks of architectural outputs need not detect [@KocherEtAl2019Spectre; @LippEtAl2018Meltdown]. Suites checking only those outputs can therefore agree while leaving the relevant information-flow property unexamined. The noninterference example in @sec-formal-bounds-sequential-equivalence explains why inspecting isolated executions is insufficient for that property. In a search loop, an objective based only on throughput or power, performance, and area (PPA) can favor changes to speculation, sharing, or mitigations without charging their security consequences. The verification plan needs checks matched to the threat model, such as a noninterference proof under declared speculative semantics, cache-timing-channel analysis, or a structural check for domain isolation. Repeating a functional test adds no direct coverage of an observation that test does not make.

## Routing Evidence Across System Layers

Qualified signals need to reach the part of the design process that can act on them. A formal counterexample may call for RTL repair or specification revision; negative timing slack calls for timing diagnosis before choosing a repair; and an unresolved empirical delta may call for expanded trace sampling. These actions change different objects, so combining every return into a scalar optimizer score would lose information needed for the next step. A *distribution shift* changes the workloads, tool versions, or operating conditions that generated the data a surrogate or claim was qualified on. A known change in those conditions, or deteriorating agreement with new reference measurements, calls for requalification of the affected surrogate (@tbl-feedback-destinations).

| **Qualified or verified status** | **Implicated architectural object** | **Eligible next technical action** |
| - | - | - |
| **Proxy outside support** | Method choice or qualification study | Recalibrate, narrow, replace, or halt proxy use. Do not generate training labels. |
| **Missing constraint** | Study formulation or representation | Record rationale and add missing constraint to representation. |
| **Resolved outcome, open mechanism** | Study formulation | Preserve result and add distinguishing contrast before altering RTL. |
| **Unresolved comparison** | Measurement plan | Use further investigation allowed by the declared plan, or define a new comparison with its own budget and stopping rule. |
| **Difference below decision margin** | Project record | Retain result without forcing architectural or model updates. |
| **Accepted bounded exception** | Project record and owner | Record waiver scope, rationale, compensating control, and reopening trigger. |
: **Established status determines next technical actions.** Execution failures route to environment repairs; qualified results direct representation, study, or project record revisions. {#tbl-feedback-destinations tbl-colwidths="[25,35,40]"}

Disagreement between checkers needs diagnosis before it drives a design change. Suppose a formal run reports Proved while simulation shows a miscompare. We first need to establish whether the proof covers the failing behavior under the simulation's inputs and conditions. Likewise, two proxies can rank a pair of candidates differently without either ranking identifying the cause of the disagreement. Their scope, reference agreement, and uncertainty need examination using @tbl-proxy-diagnostics. Retain both returns and their qualified limits while investigating the conflict. Until that conflict is explained, it supplies no resolved comparison or training label.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Drive Actions Only from Qualified Results"}
**The principle:** Raw simulation logs and unparsed tool reports must never directly trigger design modifications or dataset updates.

**The application:** Only qualified statuses justify repairs, revisions, no-change decisions, or technical stops.
:::

Waived violations (such as geometric design-rule waivers managed via Siemens Calibre Auto-Waivers) must retain explicit technical rationale, bounding spatial coordinates, compensating controls, and reopening triggers rather than converting failed checks into unconditional passes [@SiemensCalibreAutoWaivers].

## Propagating Feedback into Optimizer State

Routing qualified evidence updates the project's durable design record, but automated exploration also uses feedback to adjust the search algorithms themselves. When feedback modifies learned surrogates, generator prompts, or reinforcement learning policies, a new hazard emerges. Unverified returns, transient execution errors, or biased candidate distributions can corrupt the optimizer's internal models. Closing search loops responsibly therefore requires an explicit framework separating *durable architectural retention* from *quarantined optimizer state* (@tbl-retention-vs-quarantine).

Quarantine means storing a proposed model or policy update without letting it steer the active search. A shadow model registry holds these candidate versions alongside the data and settings needed to evaluate them. Before a version is promoted into active use, its predictions or search decisions must be qualified on protected reference cases that were not used to produce the update. This separation lets an architect test whether learning improved the method before the changed method begins selecting the next designs.

| **Dimension** | **Durable architectural retention** | **Quarantined optimizer state** |
| - | - | - |
| **Target repository** | Version-controlled project record and provenance log. | Isolated training buffer and shadow model registry. |
| **Admitted artifacts** | Checked physical signoff reports, verified SVA proofs, and frozen product requirements documents (PRDs). | Intermediate generator prompts, surrogate weights, and search trajectories. |
| **Contamination guard** | Immutable cryptographic commit hashes; audit log isolation. | Holdout evaluation sets protected from iterative gradient updates. |
| **Reopening trigger** | Changed process corner, tool behavior, or ISA assumptions; license availability separately affects whether a rerun can execute. | Changed input conditions, or drift in residuals or empirical interval coverage measured against reference results. |
: **Feedback separation prevents optimizer feedback contamination.** Durable project lineage records verified signoff evidence, while quarantined optimizer state isolates learned heuristics to prevent self-reinforcing bias. {#tbl-retention-vs-quarantine tbl-colwidths="[20,40,40]"}

Surrogate models and search heuristics must be versioned and quarantined before deployment to prevent hidden feedback loops and policy-induced dataset bias [@SculleyEtAl2015Hidden; @Settles2009ActiveLearning]. An autonomous agent refining a generation prompt based on an untested surrogate score writes strictly to quarantined state; an agent logging a formal exception for a failed timing path backed by a cryptographically sealed SDC timing waiver manifest writes directly to the durable project record. Holdout benchmarks must remain untouched or refreshed to avoid adaptive-reuse overfitting [@DworkEtAl2015ReusableHoldout].

Changes in workloads, tool versions, or PVT corners can invalidate the qualification on which dependent architectural claims rest [@QuinoneroCandelaEtAl2009DatasetShift]. Conformal prediction makes the need for reference measurements particularly clear. A conformal interval's coverage guarantee rests on exchangeability, the assumption that the calibration points and the point being predicted are drawn from one distribution in no particular order.[^fn-stats-conformal-prerequisites-c07] A latency surrogate calibrated on compute-bound SPEC CPU traces and then queried on irregular graph-analytics workloads with heavy cache-miss streams no longer has that assurance. Under such a shift, empirical coverage, the fraction of new points whose true value lands inside the interval, can fall below the nominal level $1-\alpha$ the surrogate was calibrated to; nothing in the interval itself reports the fall [@TibshiraniEtAl2019CovariateShift]. The constructed coverage figure in @sec-support-limits illustrates this failure when the workload regime leaves the calibrated range.

Rolling empirical coverage measured against reference results can reveal the loss of coverage. That monitoring observes only the cases for which new reference results are collected, so a known change in operating conditions is itself reason to revisit qualification rather than wait for an alarm. The surrogate goes back through the proxy diagnostics of @tbl-proxy-diagnostics, matched reference measurements are taken at the new stratum, and its scores are trusted again only within the region those measurements cover. Widening a reported interval alone does not restore its coverage guarantee. Tracing claims to exact execution bindings limits the rerun work to the checks affected by the change.

[^fn-stats-conformal-prerequisites-c07]: **Conformal prediction prerequisites**: Guarantees require exchangeability (permutation invariance of sequence joint distributions) and valid nonconformity scores. Workload shifts and process variations frequently violate exchangeability in hardware design, requiring runtime monitoring.

What a qualified result should change differs by scope. Within the run, it informs the next proposal. A realizable counterexample can become a constraint in the represented state, and the next generated candidate must be checked for the same protocol omission. A proxy found outside its support narrows the region the optimizer may trust; an unresolved delta may justify more samples rather than a design change. Across the project, the result changes the record. A Proved status discharges a scoped requirement, a waiver enters with its reopening trigger, and a result below the decision margin is retained without forcing an update. For later work, the useful material extends beyond surrogate weights or a winning configuration. The check that caught a defect, the mutant set that exposed a vacuous testbench, and the conditions under which a proxy was calibrated can guide a new study, subject to qualification in that setting.

Which of those retained items still holds when the workload, tool chain, or process node changes is the question distribution shift poses across problems rather than within one, and @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack takes it up under that name.

## Open Questions

Qualification exposes limits that remain difficult to bound as search changes the candidates, interfaces, and conditions being checked.

- **How can a timing surrogate bound false acceptance near zero slack?** A symmetric error measure assigns equal loss to 50\ ps of optimism and 50\ ps of pessimism, although the first can admit a timing violation and the second can reject a feasible candidate. Qualification on a fixed sample does not settle the risk when search repeatedly selects candidates near the optimistic edge. The unresolved problem is whether one-sided error bounds remain useful under that selection, and what reference measurements are needed to detect when their assumptions fail. This concerns the safety of the screening decision; the surrogate does not acquire the scope of a signoff timer.

- **How can a verification plan bound the blind spots its checks share?** Joint mutation testing exposes faults that escape both a simulation testbench and a formal assertion suite. Yet the mutants may encode the same interpretation of an ambiguous specification as both checkers, leaving an omitted requirement untouched. Independently developed contracts and challenges to specification assumptions could expose different gaps. The open issue is what coverage those methods can justify beyond the tested faults, especially when a generator introduces an interface the original verification plan did not anticipate.

- **How can early feedback qualify a new power-gating organization?** Static UPF checks can qualify declared power intent and structural isolation while leaving transient voltage droop and ground bounce during simultaneous domain wakeup unresolved. The chapter assigns those effects to physical analysis, but a search loop must choose which organizations to advance before every candidate receives detailed analysis. The research question is how conservative early models can identify unsafe wakeup behavior at useful cost, and which changes to domain structure or activity require renewed physical evaluation. A useful answer must state where the early model remains undecided.

- **When can a failed interface contract support a local repair?** Assume-guarantee reasoning separates a block's obligations from its assumptions about neighboring blocks. A failed assertion can nevertheless leave open whether to repair an internal transition, change the driving logic, or revise an inadequate contract. Diagnostic traces and targeted changes can distinguish some of these explanations, but may also reveal interacting causes. The unresolved issue is when that evidence is sufficient for local automated repair and when the system must investigate a coordinated interface redesign.

- **When is another checker worth its evaluation cost?** A checker can detect faults missed by the current suite, but its errors may also overlap with existing checks or reject useful candidates.
